_about: Operational settings for Phase 2 (allocation, overflow routing, vector-control simulator). The dataset has supply NEEDS per case count, but it has NO bed capacity, stock levels, crew numbers or crew effect. Every entry marked kind=assumption is a planning assumption chosen by the team, not data, and can be changed here without touching code. kind=data_rule means the value is computed from the dataset by the stated rule.

basis.why: Plan supplies for the model's central forecast by default. 'range_high' (top of the 80% range) is the cautious option for officers who prefer to over-stock; it is a choice, not a different model.

rounding.why: Forecasts are expected values (e.g. 3.4 cases); supplies are bought for whole patients, so the forecast is rounded half up to a case count before the case -> supplies lookup (src/supplies.py).

full_stock_basis.why: The dataset has no warehouse stock numbers. So 100% stock means 'exactly enough for every ward's forecast demand this week', and the 30-100% slider scales that down to simulate shortage. Available units per item = floor(stock_pct / 100 x total required).

full_stock_units.why: Optional fixed regional stock per item (units at 100%). null = use full_stock_basis. Fill these in when a real warehouse count is known.

stock_pct_range.why: Range of the scarcity slider required by the Phase 2 brief.

tier_weight.why: The brief asks to prioritise high-risk, high-density wards. Priority score = tier weight x population_density_sqkm. Equal steps keep it simple to explain: a Critical ward counts 4x a Low ward of the same density.

tie_break.why: Same inputs must give the same allocation (offline determinism), so equal scores are ordered by ward_id.

fill_rule.why: Wards are filled in priority order, each to 100% of its need, until an item runs out; the next ward may get a partial fill and the rest get none. Shortage therefore lands only on the lowest-priority wards, and any ward under 100% is flagged critical.

total_default.why: No crew numbers in the data. 20 crews (about one per three wards) is a starting value for the 'Total spraying crews' control; officers set the real number.

max_per_ward.why: Stops all crews piling onto one ward; beyond a few crews per ward, extra teams mostly overlap the same streets.

min_predicted_cases.why: A ward forecast below one case gets no crew; crews go where the model expects transmission.

assignment_rule.why: Crews are handed out one at a time. Each goes to the ward with the highest (priority score x predicted cases) / (crews already there + 1), ties by ward_id. A second crew in the same ward counts half as much as the first, so crews spread across busy wards instead of stacking.

model_input.why: Larvicide and drain-clearing crews remove standing water where Aedes mosquitoes breed, so the simulator lowers the ward's water_logging_risk_index (effective breeding habitat) and re-runs the Phase 1 models at 2, 3 and 4 weeks. It is the one crew-changeable input all three models use: the 2- and 3-week models use no case history at all, and the 4-week model's city case rates are cases already reported, which a crew cannot undo. Checked on 2025 peak weeks: lowering it never raises any ward's forecast.

reduction_per_crew.why: Each crew lowers the ward's water-logging index by 15% of its value (2 crews 30%, 3 crews 45%). No intervention data exists, so this effect size is a stated assumption and the UI must say so; officers can change it here.

max_total_reduction.why: Caps the combined effect at 50% so stacked crews cannot remove all breeding sites in the simulation.

rule.why: No bed capacity in the data. Each ward's capacity = the 95th percentile of its weekly hospital_beds_required in the training years (2016-2021), rounded up, at least 2. A ward is then over capacity only in its worst ~5% of weeks, which is when overflow routing should trigger. Training years only, so the validation and test years do not leak into the rule.

beds_available_pct.unit: percent of each ward's bed capacity
beds_available_pct.why: Hospital beds are shared with non-dengue patients (other illness, injuries, births), so in a bad week only part of a ward's beds can take dengue cases. This control sets that share: capacity used = floor(capacity x pct / 100), at least 1 bed. 100% is the plain rule above; lower values let officers test a squeeze. Because dengue peaks hit every ward of a city in the same weeks, at 100% the forecast rarely exceeds capacity and routing seldom triggers; at lower shares it does.

same_city_only.why: Required by the Phase 2 brief: patients are only moved between wards of the same city (Dhaka North, Dhaka South, Chattogram, Gazipur, Narayanganj), never across cities.

sender_order.why: When a city does not have enough free beds for everyone, the wards with the biggest overflow are helped first, ties by ward_id. Any patients left without a bed are then in the wards with the smallest overflow, where a few extra beds or a nearby hospital are easiest to find.

receiver_order.why: 'Lower burden' is read as 'most free beds left', ties by ward_id: it fills the wards with the most spare room first and keeps the number of transfers small. A ward at 18 of 20 beds therefore receives before an empty 1-bed ward.
